title: Testing with node:test
summary: Write and run tests with Node's built-in test runner and assert module: describe and it, hooks, strict assertions, mock functions and HTTP tests against the Express API.
introduction: Tests are the fastest way to find out whether a change broke something, and in Node they need no extra packages: the `node:test` runner and the `node:assert` module have been stable since Node 20. This lesson starts with a pure function, reads the runner's output carefully (including what a failure looks like), then moves to the two cases that matter most in a server: replacing a dependency with a mock, and sending real HTTP requests to the Express app from a test.
learningObjectives: Write tests with test, describe, it and hooks and run them with node --test
Use strict assertions and read the spec reporter's output for passes and failures
Replace dependencies with mock functions and test an Express app over HTTP

blocks.text: The code under test is a small shopping-cart module. It is deliberately free of I/O, which is what makes it easy to test: give it inputs, check outputs.

blocks.title: cart.js

blocks.text: Test files live next to the code or in a `test` folder and end in `.test.js`; `node --test` finds them by those conventions. `describe` groups related tests, `it` (an alias of `test`) defines one, and `beforeEach` gives every test a fresh cart so they cannot influence each other. The `node:assert/strict` import makes every comparison use `===` semantics:

blocks.text: With `"test": "node --test"` in `package.json`, `npm test` runs the same thing. Add `--watch` while developing to rerun on every save, and pass a file path (`node --test cart.test.js`) to run one file.

rows: Objects and arrays have the same structure and values

blocks.text: Change the expected total to `25` and run again. The runner marks the test with a cross, prints what was compared, points at the failing line and exits with code 1, which is what makes `npm test` fail a CI pipeline:

blocks.title: The test that cannot fail
blocks.text: An async test must `await` every promise it starts. `it('rejects', () => { assert.rejects(save()) })` without `await` ends before the assertion has settled: the runner can report the test as passed, and a failing assertion then surfaces later as a confusing unhandled rejection instead of a clear failure. The same happens when a `fetch` inside a test is not awaited. Make the callback `async`, `await` every assertion that returns a promise, and distrust any test that passed the first time you wrote it.

Code that sends email or writes to a payment API should not do so during a test. `mock.fn()` creates a function that records how it was called, so you can pass it in place of the real dependency and assert on the calls afterwards:

blocks.title: notify.test.js
node --test notify.test.js (summary shortened)
blocks.content:
✔ notifies once for a large order (1.0231ms)
ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 1
ℹ fail 0
...

blocks.text: `mock.method(object, 'name')` replaces an existing method the same way and restores it when the test ends, and `mock.timers` lets a test fast-forward `setTimeout` instead of really waiting.

To test Express routes, export the app from one module and keep `listen` in another (`server.js`), so a test can start the app on a random free port, send real requests with `fetch` and stop it afterwards. Port `0` asks the operating system for any free port, which keeps parallel test runs from colliding:

blocks.title: api.test.js
node --test api.test.js (summary shortened)
blocks.content:
✔ GET /api/books returns the list (24.1180ms)
✔ GET /api/books/999 returns 404 with an error message (3.4052ms)
ℹ tests 2
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 2
ℹ fail 0
...

blocks.text: `once(server, 'listening')` from `node:events` turns the event into a promise, so the test file waits until the port is bound before building `base`. The `after` hook closes the server when the file's tests are done; without it the process would stay alive and `node --test` would hang.

blocks.title: What to test first
blocks.text: Start with the pure logic (prices, validation, parsing), where tests are fast and failures are precise. Add a handful of HTTP tests for the routes that matter most, and let the database tests use `new DatabaseSync(':memory:')` so each run starts clean. `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` prints which lines no test reached.

questions.question: Importing `assert` from `node:assert/___` makes `assert.equal` compare with `===` instead of `==`.
questions.explanation: The strict variant of the module makes equal and deepEqual behave like strictEqual and deepStrictEqual, avoiding surprises from loose equality.

questions.question: Why does the HTTP test call `app.listen(0)` instead of `app.listen(3000)`?
questions.explanation: Port 0 tells the operating system to pick any free port, so the tests never fail because a development server or another test run already occupies 3000.
options: Port 0 disables networking so the test runs faster
The operating system assigns a free port, avoiding clashes with other processes
Express requires port 0 in test mode
